overview.description: Apple scab is a major foliar and fruit fungal disease of Malus species, causing olive-green to dark velvety lesions that can lead to severe premature defoliation and unmarketable, cracked fruit.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Olive-green, velvety, circular or irregular lesions appearing on the upper leaf surface, frequently initiating along major veins.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Spots begin with indistinct, feathery margins and transition to dark olive-brown or black corky lesions. Affected leaves may twist, curl, yellow, and drop prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Primary infections occur in early spring during green tip. Secondary conidia cycles multiply rapidly through summer rainy periods.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (dark scab spots that crack and distort growth), flower sepals, blossoms, and young green twigs.

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Venturia inaequalis (Cooke) G. Winter (anamorph Spilocaea pomi)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (55°F–75°F / 13°C–24°C), high humidity, and continuous foliar wetness periods of 6 to 24+ hours (Mills infection period).
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind-borne ascospores ejected from overwintered leaf litter in spring; rain-splashed conidia during the summer growing season.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Dense, unpruned canopies, prolonged leaf wetness from overhead watering, and planting highly susceptible cultivars ('McIntosh', 'Gala', 'Honeycrisp', 'Cortland').

management.cultural_practices: Prune trees annually during winter dormancy to open the canopy for sunlight and air circulation. Remove or shred fallen leaves to accelerate breakdown.
management.sanitation: Apply 5% urea spray to fallen leaves in late autumn or flail-mow leaf litter to destroy overwintering pseudothecia.
management.environmental_control: Space trees appropriately based on rootstock vigor; irrigate using drip lines rather than overhead sprinklers.
management.professional_advice: Consult local university agricultural extension fruit specialists for biofix timing models and integrated resistance management recommendations.
management.general_treatments: Protective copper sprays applied at green tip; captan, mancozeb, or biofungicides (e.g., Bacillus subtilis) applied preventatively before rain events.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Meticulous sanitation of orchard floor leaf litter eliminates the vast majority of primary spring inoculum.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Avoid overhead watering; irrigate early in the day so foliage dries rapidly in the sun.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout the lower and interior canopy 7 to 10 days after primary rain infection periods.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant scab-resistant cultivars carrying Vf genetic resistance (e.g., 'Liberty', 'Freedom', 'Enterprise', 'Pristine', 'GoldRush', 'CrimsonCrisp').

overview.description: Black rot is a destructive fungal pathogen affecting apple leaves (where it causes frog-eye leaf spot), fruit (causing firm black decay with concentric rings), and limbs (producing perennial cankers).

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small purple specks that enlarge into circular spots with tan/gray centers and distinct purple-brown outer margins resembling a frog's eye.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Circular 3–6 mm necrotic spots with defined concentric zoning and pycnidia appearing as tiny black dots within older lesions.
symptoms.progression: Foliar frog-eye spots appear 1–3 weeks after petal fall; unmanaged infections can lead to premature leaf drop and fruit infection.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (blossom-end firm rot turning coal-black and mummified), branches, and scaffold limbs (sunken perennial cankers).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm (68°F–80°F / 20°C–27°C), wet, and humid conditions; tree stress, drought, and winter injury heighten infection.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Rain splash and air currents dispersing conidia and ascospores from overwintered limb cankers, dead mummified fruit, and dead wood.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Presence of fire blight cankers, dead wood, mummified apples left on the tree, and winter bark injury.

management.cultural_practices: Prune out dead branches, fire blight strikes, and cankers at least 6–8 inches below visible margins during dormant pruning.
management.sanitation: Remove and burn or bury all mummified apples remaining on the tree or orchard floor; eliminate nearby wild brambles and dead brush.
management.environmental_control: Optimize tree vigor through balanced fertilization; avoid excess nitrogen which produces succulent, susceptible tissue.
management.professional_advice: Consult local fruit extension specialists when large scaffold cankers threaten tree structure.
management.general_treatments: Protective fungicides (captan, thiophanate-methyl, or mancozeb) applied from tight cluster through midsummer cover sprays.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Meticulous elimination of dead wood and mummified fruit completely disrupts the primary inoculum reservoir.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Keep foliage dry; manage weeds to promote lower canopy airflow.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Inspect trees following petal fall for frog-eye spots and inspect limbs for cracking cankers.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Cultivars vary in susceptibility; 'Honeycrisp' and 'Gala' require vigilant sanitation, while 'Enterprise' displays moderate tolerance.

overview.description: Cedar apple rust is a heteroecious fungal disease that requires both an apple or crabapple host and an Eastern red cedar or juniper host to complete its complex two-year life cycle.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on the upper leaf surface that gradually turn reddish-orange and develop tiny dark dots (spermogonia).
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Upper leaf surface displays vibrant orange-yellow spots; by midsummer, the underside of the leaf directly beneath spots swells and erupts with tube-like spore structures (aecia).
symptoms.progression: Infections occur in spring during rainy periods; aecia release aeciospores in late summer that infect junipers, producing woody galls that mature over 18 months.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (orange lesions with raised margins near the calyx) and green twigs.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Spring temperatures of 50°F–75°F (10°C–24°C) accompanying rainfall that causes cedar galls to extrude gelatinous orange telial horns.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind-borne basidiospores carried from gelatinous cedar galls to apple foliage, often over distances of several hundred yards up to 2 miles.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Proximity to Eastern red cedars (Juniperus virginiana) and planting highly susceptible apple cultivars.

management.cultural_practices: Remove Eastern red cedar trees within a 1- to 2-mile radius of the orchard where practical, or prune out woody galls from nearby ornamental junipers.
management.sanitation: Inspect neighboring landscape junipers in late winter and prune off golf-ball sized brown cedar galls before spring rains.
management.environmental_control: Improve canopy ventilation to facilitate rapid leaf drying following spring showers.
management.professional_advice: Consult extension services if cedar trees cannot be removed from adjacent property boundaries.
management.general_treatments: Protective sterol-inhibiting fungicides (myclobutanil) or mancozeb applied from pink bud through petal fall when telial horns are gelatinized.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Eradicate cedar galls on ornamental junipers before orange spore horns emerge in spring.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Minimize overhead wetness; rely on ground irrigation.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Monitor local red cedar trees in spring for the emergence of gelatinous orange tentacles.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant immune or highly resistant apple cultivars (e.g., 'Liberty', 'Freedom', 'Enterprise', 'Redfree', 'William's Pride'). Avoid 'Rome Beauty', 'Golden Delicious', and 'Gala' near cedars.

overview.description: The specimen exhibits characteristics typical of healthy apple foliage, with uniform pigmentation and absence of visible lesions associated with the modeled fungal and bacterial pathogens.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Normal deep green foliage, crisp intact margins, and uniform leaf blade architecture without chlorosis, necrosis, or spotting.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No necrotic lesions, fungal sporulation, powdery growth, or bacterial water-soaking observed.
symptoms.progression: Foliage maintains full photosynthetic and transpiration function under balanced cultural management.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Appropriate sunlight, well-drained loam soil, adequate moisture, and balanced orchard nutrition.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Environmental stressors, drought, or canopy crowding can predispose foliage to latent pathogens.

management.cultural_practices: Maintain regular annual winter pruning to sustain open vase or central leader canopy architecture.
management.sanitation: Rake and compost or shred fallen leaves each autumn to prevent buildup of overwintering fungal spores.
management.environmental_control: Maintain balanced soil pH (6.0–6.8) and apply irrigation during prolonged midsummer dry spells.
management.professional_advice: Consult local extension services for routine soil testing and seasonal preventative spray programs.
management.general_treatments: No curative chemical intervention required for healthy specimens.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Keep the orchard understory mowed and clean of brush and dropped fruit.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip or under-canopy micro-sprinklers to keep leaves completely dry.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Conduct biweekly leaf inspections throughout the growing season to detect early pest or disease signs.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Maintain certified disease-free rootstocks and scions.

references.title: Apple Production Guide - Tree Health and Nutrition

overview.description: The specimen displays normal healthy highbush blueberry foliage with uniform green pigmentation, smooth margins, and absence of foliar leaf spots or rusts.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Vibrant green, leathery leaves with smooth intact margins and absence of chlorosis, red ringspots, or necrotic lesions.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No fungal leaf spotting, rust pustules, or anthracnose blighting present.
symptoms.progression: Sustains healthy vegetative growth and fruit ripening.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.2), high organic matter, pine bark mulch, and regular, uniform moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: High soil pH (>5.5) induces iron chlorosis; poor drainage causes Phytophthora root rot.

management.cultural_practices: Maintain soil acidity with elemental sulfur or ammonium sulfate fertilizers; maintain 3–4 inches of aged pine bark mulch.
management.sanitation: Prune out older non-productive canes (over 5 years old) during dormancy to stimulate vigorous young canes.
management.environmental_control: Ensure well-drained, raised beds to prevent standing water.
management.professional_advice: Submit annual soil and foliar tissue tests to cooperative extension labs to monitor soil pH and micronutrients.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Keep rows weed-free and replenish organic mulch annually.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Drip irrigation is essential; avoid wetting foliage to prevent anthracnose and leaf rust.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout weekly from bud break through harvest for spotted wing drosophila and fungal spotting.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant certified virus-indexed cultivars adapted to your chilling hour zone.

overview.description: Powdery mildew of sweet and tart cherry affects leaves and green fruit, producing white superficial mycelial mats that cause leaf curling, stunted shoot growth, and unmarketable fruit.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Circular patches of white, powdery fungal growth developing on the undersides of leaves, rapidly spreading across the leaf blade.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Superficial white powdery patches; leaves curl upward, become distorted, and can turn brittle or drop prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Initiates in late spring on new sucker growth and interior canopy shoots; yellow to black chasmothecia (overwintering structures) develop within mycelial mats by late summer.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (developing white powdery web-like patches, fruit deformation, and delayed ripening), shoot tips, and petioles.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm (60°F–80°F / 15°C–27°C), dry air with high relative humidity within dense canopies; unlike most fungi, it does not require free water on leaves to germinate.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Airborne conidia carried by wind currents from active colonies; ascospores released from overwintering chasmothecia in spring.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Dense, shaded canopies, excessive nitrogen fertilization causing lush vegetative growth, and low airflow.

management.cultural_practices: Prune cherry trees to improve light penetration and airflow; remove basal suckers and water sprouts that harbor early powdery mildew.
management.sanitation: Disinfect pruning tools and remove severely infected terminal shoots.
management.environmental_control: Avoid excessive nitrogen applications that promote overly dense succulent shoot flushes.
management.professional_advice: Consult tree fruit extension specialists for rotational fungicide schedules to prevent strobilurin or DMI resistance.
management.general_treatments: Sulfur sprays (where temperature permits, avoiding phytotoxicity above 85°F), potassium bicarbonate, or horticultural oils applied at shuck fall.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Prune out diseased shoots during dormant and summer pruning cycles.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use micro-sprinklers or drip lines; keep irrigation water away from the lower tree canopy.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Regularly inspect the undersides of young leaves in the lower canopy starting at shuck split.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select less susceptible cherry cultivars; tart cherries ('Montmorency') require vigilant preventative management.

references.title: Cherry Powdery Mildew Pest Management Guidelines

overview.description: The specimen exhibits typical healthy cherry foliage with dark green glossy upper surfaces, serrated intact margins, and absence of powdery mildew, leaf spot, or bacterial canker.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Glossy green leaves with uniform coloration, prominent veining, and intact margins.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No fungal powder, shot-hole perforations, leaf spot lesions, or bacterial gummosis present.
symptoms.progression: Normal vegetative canopy development supporting fruit bud set.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sun, deep well-drained sandy loam soil, adequate winter chilling, and consistent moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Over-fertilization, poor drainage, or physical bark wounds predispose trees to bacterial canker.

management.cultural_practices: Prune sweet cherries in summer dry weather to reduce bacterial canker risk; prune tart cherries in late winter.
management.sanitation: Rake and compost fallen leaves to minimize overwintering cherry leaf spot inoculum.
management.environmental_control: Maintain adequate tree spacing and maintain orchard ground cover.
management.professional_advice: Consult extension specialists for diagnostic evaluation if sudden dieback or gummosis occurs.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Sterilize pruning tools with 70% ethanol or 10% bleach between trees.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Irrigate at the ground level; avoid wetting leaves or trunk flare.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout weekly from petal fall through post-harvest for leaf spot or powdery mildew.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant certified virus-free rootstocks and scions.

references.title: Sweet Cherry Production and Orchard Management

overview.description: Gray leaf spot is a widespread, yield-limiting foliar fungal disease of corn characterized by distinct rectangular, vein-bounded necrotic lesions that coalesce to cause extensive leaf blighting.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small tan spots that expand into elongated, strictly rectangular necrotic lesions bounded precisely by parallel leaf veins.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions are 0.5 to 2 inches long, blocky, tan to gray, with sharp parallel margins defined by leaf veins. When humid, lesions turn gray from fungal sporulation.
symptoms.progression: Symptoms typically begin on lower leaves around tasseling and progress upward; extensive blighting can destroy the ear leaf and upper canopy.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Leaf sheaths and ear husks in severe outbreaks; stalk lodging may follow premature defoliation.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75°F–85°F / 24°C–30°C), persistent high relative humidity (>90%), and extended morning dew or leaf wetness periods of 12+ hours.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia originating from infested crop residue on the soil surface.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Continuous corn-on-corn planting, conservation or no-till practices leaving heavy surface residue, and planting susceptible hybrids.

management.cultural_practices: Rotate out of corn for at least 1–2 years to non-host crops (soybeans, small grains) to allow infested residue to decompose.
management.sanitation: Tillage practices that incorporate crop residue into the soil accelerate decomposition where conservation plans permit.
management.environmental_control: Optimize planting density to promote canopy air movement and faster drying.
management.professional_advice: Consult local agronomy extension agents regarding economic thresholds for foliar fungicide application between VT (tasseling) and R2 (blister).
management.general_treatments: Strobilurin (QoI), triazole (DMI), or SDHI mixed-mode fungicides applied at tasseling (VT/R1) when scouting indicates disease presence on the third leaf below the ear.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Crop rotation and residue management are the primary cultural defenses.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Avoid evening overhead irrigation cycles that extend overnight foliar dew periods.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout lower leaves every 7–10 days starting at V10 growth stage through pollination.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select commercial corn hybrids with high genetic tolerance or quantitative resistance ratings against Gray Leaf Spot.

overview.description: Common rust is an airborne foliar fungal disease of sweet and field corn that produces circular to elongate, powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small, scattered, circular to oval pustules (uredinia) that erupt through the epidermis on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Golden-brown to dark cinnamon pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle, releasing dusty brown urediniospores. Pustules turn blackish-brown later in the season as teliospores form.
symptoms.progression: Can appear early in the season on whorl leaves; severe infections cause chlorosis, premature senescence, and ragged leaf tearing.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Stalks, leaf sheaths, and ear husks in exceptionally severe infections.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (60°F–75°F / 16°C–24°C) with high relative humidity and 6+ hours of dew; hot summer weather (>85°F / 30°C) suppresses development.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Urediniospores are blown northward annually by weather systems from southern overwintering regions; the pathogen does not typically overwinter in freezing northern regions.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Late planting, planting susceptible sweet corn varieties or inbred lines, and persistent cool humid weather.

management.cultural_practices: Plant early in the season to allow the crop to pass critical developmental stages before rust spores arrive on southern winds.
management.sanitation: Residue destruction does not affect common rust because spores are transported long distances aerially each year.
management.environmental_control: Maintain adequate row spacing for ventilation.
management.professional_advice: Consult extension guidelines; sweet corn is substantially more vulnerable than field corn, with treatment thresholds based on pustule density per leaf.
management.general_treatments: Foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins) applied to sweet corn when pustules appear on more than 50% of plants before tasseling.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Focus on hybrid genetics; airborne long-range spore dispersal limits local sanitation efficacy.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Avoid overhead watering during late afternoon to prevent extended overnight wetness.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout leaves weekly from early whorl through silking, especially after prolonged cloudy, cool weather fronts.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant field corn hybrids and sweet corn varieties carrying specific Rp resistance genes (e.g., Rp1-D) or high general horizontal resistance.

references.title: Common and Southern Rust of Corn

overview.description: Northern corn leaf blight is a serious fungal disease of corn characterized by large, cigar-shaped, grayish-green to tan lesions that can cause massive loss of photosynthetic area and severe yield reduction.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Large, elongated, elliptical or cigar-shaped lesions (1 to 6 inches long) developing on leaves.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions begin as pale, water-soaked narrow streaks that expand into long, elliptical, grayish-green to tan lesions with rounded ends. When humid, dark olive-gray sporulation develops in the lesion centers.
symptoms.progression: Typically begins on lower leaves around flowering and progresses upward; in severe cases, leaves turn completely necrotic and die prematurely.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Ear husks in heavy outbreaks; secondary stalk lodging often occurs due to cannibalization of stalk carbohydrates.

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Exserohilum turcicum (Pass.) K.J. Leonard & Suggs (syn. Setosphaeria turcica)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65°F–80°F / 18°C–27°C) accompanied by extended periods of leaf wetness (6 to 18 hours from heavy dew or frequent rain).
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Rain splash and wind currents dispersing conidia from overwintered corn residue left on the soil surface.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Continuous corn production, no-till residue management, late planting, and planting susceptible hybrids lacking Ht resistance genes.

management.cultural_practices: Rotate fields to non-host crops (soybean, alfalfa) for 1–2 years to promote natural decay of infested corn debris.
management.sanitation: Where soil conservation permits, chisel plow or till residue to encourage microbial decomposition of overwintering conidia.
management.environmental_control: Select planting dates and plant populations that promote canopy airflow.
management.professional_advice: Consult extension agronomy specialists when lesions are established on leaves below the ear prior to tasseling.
management.general_treatments: Foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins, SDHIs) applied between VT and R2 when scouting shows active lesions threatening upper canopy leaves.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Crop rotation and residue management significantly reduce primary spring inoculum.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Avoid late-day overhead pivot irrigation that extends nighttime foliar wetness.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout lower leaves beginning around V8–V10 through the silking stage.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant hybrids with qualitative Ht resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, HtN) or high quantitative polygenic tolerance ratings.

overview.description: The specimen displays normal healthy corn foliage characterized by upright, arching green leaves with distinct midribs and absence of foliar leaf spots, rusts, or blights.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Uniform rich green leaf blades with parallel venation, intact margins, and prominent central midrib.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No rectangular gray leaf spots, cigar-shaped blights, rust pustules, or viral striping present.
symptoms.progression: Sustains active vegetative elongation, tasseling, and grain fill.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm growing season (70°F–86°F), full sunlight, well-drained fertile soil, and adequate nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Severe drought, nitrogen deficiency (V-shaped yellowing down midrib), or hail injury can weaken plants.

management.cultural_practices: Follow sound fertility programs based on routine soil testing; maintain optimal plant population density.
management.sanitation: Practice multi-year crop rotations with soybeans or legumes to maintain soil health.
management.environmental_control: Optimize field drainage and manage weed competition early in the season (V1–V6).
management.professional_advice: Consult local crop consultants for scouting weed thresholds and fertility tissue sampling.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Maintain rotational practices to prevent residue-borne disease build-up.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Apply irrigation to match evapotranspiration demands, particularly during pollination and grain fill.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout fields regularly throughout the growing season for emerging pests or nutrient deficiencies.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select locally adapted commercial hybrids with strong defensive disease ratings.

overview.description: Black rot is one of the most destructive fungal diseases of cultivated grapes in warm, humid regions, attacking all green vine tissues and completely shriveling berries into hard, black, mummified raisins.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small, circular, reddish-brown spots with dark brown margins developing on leaves in late spring.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions are 2 to 10 mm in diameter, with reddish-brown centers and defined dark borders; as lesions mature, tiny black pimple-like structures (pycnidia) appear arranged in a ring just inside the margin.
symptoms.progression: Foliar lesions appear first; berry infection occurs from bloom through 4–6 weeks post-bloom, turning grapes soft, brown, and then rapidly shriveling into black, wrinkled mummies.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit clusters, shoot canes, tendrils, and leaf petioles (producing elongated, sunken black cankers).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm (70°F–85°F / 21°C–29°C), humid, and rainy weather; infection requires only 6 to 9 hours of continuous leaf wetness at optimal temperatures.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Ascospores discharged from overwintered mummified berries on the ground or retained on the trellis; rain-splashed conidia from cane lesions during the growing season.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Dense vine canopies, retention of mummified fruit clusters on the vine, lack of early spring fungicide protection, and planting susceptible Vitis vinifera or French hybrid cultivars.

management.cultural_practices: Prune vines during dormancy and meticulously remove all mummified berries from the canopy and trellis wires; disk or cultivate vineyard floor to bury fallen mummies.
management.sanitation: Prune out infected cane cankers and destroy or compost all pruned brush.
management.environmental_control: Employ canopy management techniques (shoot thinning, leaf pulling around clusters) to enhance sunlight and airflow.
management.professional_advice: Consult viticulture extension specialists for disease-forecasting spray models and resistance management.
management.general_treatments: Fungicide protection is critical from early shoot growth (1–3 inches) through 4 weeks post-bloom using mancozeb, captan, myclobutanil, or azoxystrobin.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Complete eradication of mummified berries from the trellis eliminates the primary source of spring ascospores.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation; avoid any overhead watering that wets grape clusters.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout lower leaves beginning at bud break and examine fruit clusters closely following bloom.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Vitis vinifera and French hybrids are generally susceptible; some native American cultivars ('Concord', 'Norton') show varying degrees of tolerance.

overview.description: Esca (black measles) is a complex, destructive grapevine trunk disease caused by a succession of xylem-inhabiting fungi that produce distinctive tiger-striped foliar chlorosis, berry speckling, and internal wood decay.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis creating a distinctive 'tiger-stripe' pattern, where green tissue remains only along the main veins while interveinal areas yellow and dry out.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Foliar stripes transition from yellow/red to scorched brown necrotic bands; leaves may drop prematurely leaving bare shoot tips.
symptoms.progression: Chronic form exhibits gradual foliar tiger-striping and berry speckling year after year; acute form ('apoplexy') causes sudden complete vine collapse and wilting in hot midsummer.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (small dark brown to purple sunken spots across the berry surface resembling measles) and trunk wood (internal dark vascular streaking and spongy white rot).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Fungal complex including Phaeoacremonium minimum, Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, and basidiomycete wood-rot fungi (Fomitiporia species).
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Hot midsummer temperatures trigger acute symptoms in water-stressed vines; spore infections occur primarily in winter through fresh pruning wounds during rain.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind- and rain-borne spores enter vascular vessels via open pruning cuts on trunks and cordons; contaminated nursery propagation material can also spread the disease.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Large pruning cuts made during rainy winter periods, older vineyards (>8–10 years), and vine water stress.

management.cultural_practices: Delay winter pruning until late in the dormant season (late February/March) when wound healing is rapid; paint or spray large pruning wounds with wound protectants.
management.sanitation: Mark symptomatic vines during summer; in winter, retrain new suckers from the base and saw off diseased trunks below infected wood (trunk renewal).
management.environmental_control: Avoid severe vine water stress during hot periods through balanced drip irrigation.
management.professional_advice: Consult viticulture specialists for diagnostic vascular wood analysis and surgical trunk renewal techniques.
management.general_treatments: There are no curative chemical fungicides once fungi are established in trunk wood; apply wound sealants or biofungicides (Trichoderma) to fresh pruning cuts.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Sterilize pruning shears when moving between symptomatic and healthy vines.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Maintain regular drip irrigation schedules to prevent heat-stress-induced apoplexy.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Survey vineyards in midsummer (July–August) for characteristic tiger-striped foliage and spotted berries.
prevention.resistant_varieties: All major Vitis vinifera cultivars are susceptible, but 'Cabernet Sauvignon', 'Sauvignon Blanc', and 'Chardonnay' are especially vulnerable.

overview.description: Grape leaf blight is a late-season foliar fungal disease that causes angular, dark brown to black leaf spots with chlorotic margins, leading to premature defoliation and poor vine cold-hardening.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Angular, irregular reddish-brown to black spots (2–8 mm) bounded by small leaf veins, typically appearing on older canopy leaves in mid-to-late summer.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions are sharply defined, dark brown on the upper leaf surface, with olive-gray to black velvety fungal sporulation on the underside during humid weather.
symptoms.progression: Begins in the interior lower canopy and moves upward; extensive lesion coalescence causes leaves to blight, curl, dry out, and drop prematurely before harvest.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Leaf petioles, young shoot stems, and occasionally fruit pedicels.

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (anamorph Isariopsis clavispora / Phaeoisariopsis clavispora)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75°F–85°F / 24°C–30°C) with persistent high humidity and rainy conditions in mid-to-late summer.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind and splashing rain disperse conidia produced on overwintered fallen leaves and shoot lesions.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Dense, shaded canopies, poor weed management, and vineyards with heavy late-season humidity and dew.

management.cultural_practices: Prune to improve canopy sunlight and air circulation; perform selective leaf removal in the fruiting zone.
management.sanitation: Shred or plow under fallen leaves in late autumn to accelerate decomposition of overwintering fungal structures.
management.environmental_control: Control vineyard weeds to lower relative humidity in the vine understory.
management.professional_advice: Consult viticulture extension specialists if premature defoliation occurs before berry sugar accumulation is complete.
management.general_treatments: Late-season protective fungicide applications (copper, captan, or mancozeb prior to pre-harvest intervals) where disease pressure is high.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Mow and manage vineyard floor debris to reduce spore reservoirs.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Ensure ground-directed drip irrigation is used exclusively.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout interior canopy leaves in midsummer following post-bloom spray intervals.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Evaluate local cultivar susceptibility; Vitis labrusca and hybrid varieties show variable tolerance.

overview.description: The specimen exhibits typical healthy grapevine foliage with vibrant green color, well-developed lobing, and absence of black rot, mildew, or trunk disease symptoms.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Uniform green leaf blade with healthy palmate lobes, clear veins, and crisp unblemished margins.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No fungal spotting, powdery or downy mildew patches, or tiger-striped necrosis observed.
symptoms.progression: Supports vigorous shoot growth, flowering, and veraison.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sun, well-drained gravelly or sandy loam soils, appropriate trellis training, and balanced moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Over-cropping, canopy congestion, or excessive nitrogen promote succulent growth prone to infection.

management.cultural_practices: Implement regular shoot positioning, shoot thinning, and basal leaf removal to maintain an open canopy.
management.sanitation: Prune out dead canes during dormancy and burn or chop all vine prunings.
management.environmental_control: Monitor soil moisture via tensiometers to avoid waterlogging or extreme drought.
management.professional_advice: Consult viticulture extension specialists for petiole nutrient testing and canopy balance assessments.
management.general_treatments: No curative sprays needed for healthy specimens.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Keep vine rows weed-free and trellis wires clean of old tendrils and fruit mummies.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Maintain drip irrigation; never apply overhead water to grapevines.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout vineyards weekly from bud break through harvest for early foliar signs.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select rootstocks and cultivars adapted to local climate and soil conditions.

references.title: Grape Production and Vineyard Management Guidelines

overview.description: Huanglongbing (HLB), or citrus greening, is the most destructive citrus disease in the world. It is caused by an unculturable phloem-restricted bacterium spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, leading to tree decline, bitter lopsided fruit, and tree death.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy mottle chlorosis across the leaf blade where yellowing patterns do not mirror each other on opposite sides of the midvein; corky, raised veins.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Blotchy, mottled yellow-and-green patches that cross leaf veins irregularly; leaves may be small, upright ('rabbit ears'), and display severe zinc- or iron-like deficiency patterns.
symptoms.progression: Begins with yellow shoots on a single branch ('yellow dragon') and gradually spreads throughout the entire canopy, causing extensive dieback and eventual tree death within 3–5 years.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (small, lopsided, asymmetric, remaining green at the blossom end, with dark aborted seeds and a bitter, salty taste) and roots (severe feeder root rot).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm citrus-growing climates (70°F–90°F / 21°C–32°C) that favor rapid reproduction and dispersal of psyllid insect vectors.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Vectored primarily by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri); also transmitted through infected budding wood and vegetative grafting.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: All commercial sweet orange (Citrus sinensis), grapefruit, and mandarin varieties are susceptible; proximity to infected citrus groves with unmanaged psyllid populations.

management.cultural_practices: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock from screenhouses; scout groves regularly for psyllid nymphs and adults.
management.sanitation: Eradicate and remove confirmed HLB-infected trees immediately in regions under containment programs to eliminate bacterial reservoirs.
management.environmental_control: Optimize tree nutrition (foliar micronutrients) and irrigation to support tree root health, though this does not cure the underlying bacterial infection.
management.professional_advice: Citrus greening is a quarantined agricultural disease; suspect cases must be reported immediately to state agricultural departments or university citrus extension agents.
management.general_treatments: Strict chemical or biological control of the psyllid vector (systemic neonicotinoids, organophosphates, or Tamarixia radiata parasitoid wasps).

prevention.crop_hygiene: Adhere to citrus quarantine regulations; never transport citrus plants or budwood across quarantine zones.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Maintain precise micro-irrigation to reduce root stress.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout new leaf flushes for psyllid eggs, nymphs, and white waxy excretions; use yellow sticky cards.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Currently no commercially immune sweet orange cultivars exist; ongoing research focuses on genetically engineered or gene-edited resistant rootstocks.

overview.description: Bacterial spot is a damaging bacterial disease of stone fruits, causing angular foliar lesions that drop out to produce a 'shot-hole' appearance, severe defoliation, twig cankers, and pitted fruit lesions.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small, water-soaked, angular spots (1–3 mm) that appear on the undersides of leaves and turn purple-brown to black on the upper surface.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Angular necrotic spots bounded by veinlets; the diseased centers frequently drop out, giving the leaf a ragged 'shot-hole' appearance. Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Infections appear in spring; severe defoliation weakens the tree, reduces fruit size, and increases sunburn risk.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (deep, sunken, dark craters that exude gum and crack) and twigs (spring and summer cankers).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni (Smith) Vauterin et al.
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70°F–85°F / 21°C–29°C), high humidity, frequent rainfall, and blowing sandy winds that create micro-wounds on plant surfaces.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Rain splash, wind-driven water droplets, and pruning tools; bacteria overwinter in twig cankers and terminal bud scales.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Sandy soils with blowing winds, highly susceptible peach cultivars, and overhead irrigation.

management.cultural_practices: Plant windbreaks in sandy locations to minimize abrasive wind injury to leaves and fruit; avoid high nitrogen fertilization that produces excessive lush growth.
management.sanitation: Prune out twig cankers during dormant pruning.
management.environmental_control: Ensure adequate tree spacing to facilitate rapid drying of leaves after rain.
management.professional_advice: Consult tree fruit extension specialists regarding regional copper and oxytetracycline spray timing and resistance management.
management.general_treatments: Protective copper sprays applied at leaf fall and dormant bud stages; oxytetracycline or copper sprays applied at low rates from petal fall through shuck split.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Purchase certified disease-free nursery stock.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; use under-tree drip or micro-sprinklers.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout leaves and green shoots starting 2–3 weeks after petal fall.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select resistant peach cultivars (e.g., 'Biscoe', 'Candor', 'Derby', 'Harvester', 'Reliance'). Avoid highly susceptible cultivars ('O'Henry', 'Elberta', 'Flaming Fury').

overview.description: The specimen exhibits typical healthy peach foliage with lanceolate, deep green leaves, fine serration, and absence of bacterial spot, peach leaf curl, or fungal cankers.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Vibrant green lanceolate leaves with sharp pointed tips, finely serrated margins, and uniform leaf texture.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No shot-hole perforations, reddish leaf puckering, or necrotic spotting present.
symptoms.progression: Sustains healthy tree growth, fruit sizing, and flower bud set for the following season.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sun, deep well-drained sandy loam soil, adequate winter chilling, and regular moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Poor soil drainage leads to Phytophthora root rot; winter injury predisposes trees to bacterial canker.

management.cultural_practices: Maintain open-center (vase) canopy pruning to maximize sunlight and airflow throughout the canopy.
management.sanitation: Clear fallen leaves and mummified peach fruit from the orchard floor each autumn.
management.environmental_control: Monitor soil moisture to prevent water stress during fruit sizing.
management.professional_advice: Consult tree fruit extension specialists for leaf tissue fertility analysis and dormant oil spray schedules.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Sterilize pruning tools between trees to prevent spreading vascular pathogens.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation to keep water off trunks and lower foliage.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout trees weekly from bud swell through harvest for pests and foliar diseases.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant certified virus-tested peach varieties with disease resistance suited to your region.

references.title: Peach Tree Care and Disease Management

overview.description: Bacterial spot is one of the most economically devastating diseases of bell pepper and tomato, causing foliar lesions, severe defoliation, flower drop, and raised scab-like lesions on fruit.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small (1–3 mm), circular to irregular water-soaked spots that develop on the undersides of leaves and turn dark brown to black on the upper surface.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions are dark brown, slightly raised on the lower surface, often surrounded by a narrow chlorotic halo. Severely infected leaves turn yellow, scorch, and drop prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Infection spreads rapidly during warm summer storms; extensive defoliation exposes fruit to sunscald and substantially reduces harvest yields.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (small, circular, raised, blister-like or scab-like rough brown spots) and stems (elongated dark cankers).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Xanthomonas euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, and X. gardneri
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75°F–90°F / 24°C–32°C), high humidity (>85%), and frequent driving rain or overhead sprinkler irrigation.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Contaminated seed, infected transplants, rain splash, overhead irrigation, and field workers moving through wet foliage.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Overhead irrigation, handling wet plants, planting susceptible non-resistant pepper varieties, and continuous solanaceous cropping.

management.cultural_practices: Rotate fields out of solanaceous crops (peppers, tomatoes, eggplants, potatoes) for at least 2–3 years. Avoid handling or cultivating plants when foliage is wet.
management.sanitation: Use hot-water treated or certified disease-free seed; inspect commercial transplants carefully; destroy crop residue immediately after harvest.
management.environmental_control: Use drip irrigation and plastic mulch to prevent soil splashing onto lower foliage.
management.professional_advice: Consult local extension agents regarding bacterial spot race identification (Races 1–10) in your production area.
management.general_treatments: Preventative fixed copper bactericides mixed with mancozeb, or plant-activators (acibenzolar-S-methyl / Actigard) applied early in crop development.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Sterilize seedling trays, transplant benches, and pruning shears regularly.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Never use overhead sprinklers; deliver water strictly through subsurface or surface drip lines.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout transplants before field setting and inspect field rows weekly, focusing on low spots and field edges.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant bell pepper hybrids carrying multi-race hypersensitive resistance (X10R varieties resistant to Bacterial Spot races 1–10, e.g., 'Aristotle', 'Playmaker', 'Vanguard').

references.title: Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato

overview.description: The specimen displays characteristic healthy bell pepper foliage with vibrant green, smooth, ovate leaves, strong upright stems, and absence of bacterial spot, anthracnose, or viral mottling.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Uniform deep green color, smooth ovate-to-elliptic leaf blades, crisp margins, and strong petiole attachment.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No water-soaked spots, necrotic lesions, yellow mosaic patterns, or leaf curling observed.
symptoms.progression: Maintains vigorous flowering, continuous fruit set, and uniform fruit development.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sun, daytime temperatures of 70°F–85°F (21°C–29°C), well-drained loam soil rich in organic matter, and regular drip irrigation.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Over-fertilization with nitrogen can cause blossom drop and leafy growth; water stress causes blossom end rot.

management.cultural_practices: Support heavy-fruiting pepper plants with stakes or trellis twine to prevent stem breakage. Maintain black or silver plastic mulch.
management.sanitation: Keep planting beds weed-free and remove any cull fruit from the field.
management.environmental_control: Ensure adequate soil calcium and consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom-end rot.
management.professional_advice: Consult vegetable extension agents for seasonal fertility guidelines and integrated pest management.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Disinfect stakes and trellising equipment before the growing season.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Drip irrigation is mandatory to keep foliage dry and maintain consistent root-zone moisture.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout weekly for aphids, thrips, and early foliar spots.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select multi-disease resistant hybrid pepper varieties suited to your growing season.

references.title: Pepper Production and Pest Management Guide

overview.description: Early blight is a common foliar and tuber fungal disease of potato and tomato, characterized by dark brown to black circular lesions displaying a prominent 'target-board' pattern of concentric rings.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Dark brown to black spots that develop initially on older lower leaves, often surrounded by a diffuse chlorotic yellow halo.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Circular to oval necrotic lesions with conspicuous concentric rings resembling a target board. As lesions coalesce, large areas of the leaf blade turn brown, dry out, and drop.
symptoms.progression: Appears during tuber bulking on senescing lower foliage and moves upward into the middle and upper canopy under favorable conditions.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Stems (elongated dark brown lesions) and tubers (sunken, dark, dry, leathery surface rot with a raised purple-brown border).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75°F–85°F / 24°C–30°C) alternating between wet periods (dew, rain, irrigation) and dry windy periods; stressed or nutrient-deficient plants are most vulnerable.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia; the fungus overwinters on infected crop residue in the soil and in infected seed tubers.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Crop stress (drought, nitrogen deficiency, high tuber demand), planting susceptible cultivars ('Russet Burbank'), and continuous potato cropping.

management.cultural_practices: Rotate out of solanaceous crops for at least 2–3 years. Maintain optimal nitrogen and potassium fertility to delay foliar senescence.
management.sanitation: Destroy cull potato piles and eliminate volunteer potatoes that harbor overwintering mycelium and spores.
management.environmental_control: Optimize irrigation timing to avoid extended leaf wetness.
management.professional_advice: Consult potato extension specialists to run TomCast or P-Days forecasting models to optimize fungicide spray timings.
management.general_treatments: Protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) applied before row closure; rotational applications of QoI (azoxystrobin) or SDHI fungicides where resistance has not developed.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers and disk crop residue immediately after harvest.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Irrigate in early morning so canopy dries thoroughly before nightfall.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout lower canopy leaves weekly beginning around row closure or tuber initiation.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant cultivars with moderate to high foliar resistance (e.g., 'Defender', 'Elba', 'Jacqueline Lee').

overview.description: Late blight is the devastating oomycete pathogen responsible for the historic Irish Potato Famine. It causes rapid water-soaked foliar lesions with white fuzzy sporulation, complete canopy collapse within days, and destructive tuber rot.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked, pale-to-dark green lesions that rapidly expand and turn purplish-brown to black, often with a pale chlorotic border.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Large necrotic lesions that feel water-soaked; during humid or wet conditions, a delicate white fuzzy growth (sporangia and sporangiophores) forms on the undersides of leaves at the lesion margin.
symptoms.progression: Under cool, wet conditions, the disease spreads exponentially, destroying an entire field canopy in 7 to 10 days, accompanied by a distinct decaying odor.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Stems (dark brown to black greasy water-soaked cankers) and tubers (dry granular brown rot extending irregularly into the tuber flesh).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (50°F–70°F / 10°C–21°C) with persistent high humidity (>90%) and frequent rain, fog, or heavy dew.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Airborne sporangia carried for miles on wind currents under cloudy, humid skies; water-splashed zoospores; infected seed tubers.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Proximity to infected cull piles or volunteer potatoes, cool wet microclimates, lack of preventative fungicide protection, and planting susceptible varieties.

management.cultural_practices: Destroy all cull potato piles by freezing, burying under 2+ feet of soil, or covering with black plastic. Scout fields intensively following cool rainy periods.
management.sanitation: Eradicate volunteer potatoes; kill vines completely 2–3 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber infection during digging.
management.environmental_control: Avoid planting in low, poorly drained areas subject to prolonged fog or dew.
management.professional_advice: Late blight is a community-level agricultural emergency; immediately report suspected finds to local extension specialists or USAblight diagnostic networks.
management.general_treatments: Apply preventative protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) regularly; in confirmed outbreaks, apply targeted oomycete fungicides (mandipropamid, cyazofamid, fluopicolide, oxathiapiprolin).

prevention.crop_hygiene: Plant exclusively certified disease-free seed tubers; never plant tubers showing reddish-brown surface decay.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Avoid overhead watering during cool, overcast weather; allow vines to dry before sunset.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Monitor regional disease tracking networks (e.g., USAblight.org) and scout low-lying field sections biweekly.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant cultivars with late blight resistance genes (e.g., 'Elba', 'Defender', 'Missaukee', 'Sarpo Mira').
