overview.description: The specimen displays normal healthy potato foliage with compound dark green leaves, smooth margins, and absence of early blight concentric rings, late blight water-soaking, or viral mosaic.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Compound pinnate leaves with rich green leaflets, smooth undulating margins, and sturdy succulent stems.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No target-board lesions, water-soaked margins, white mold, or leaf curl observed.
symptoms.progression: Supports active tuber initiation, flowering, and rapid tuber bulking.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Cool temperate climates (60°F–70°F), loose well-drained sandy loam soil, acidic pH (5.0–6.5 to suppress scab), and consistent moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Over-watering causes root hypoxia and blackleg; low potassium accelerates leaf senescence.

management.cultural_practices: Hill potatoes properly to prevent greening of tubers and maintain loose soil for root expansion.
management.sanitation: Control solanaceous weeds (nightshade) that serve as alternate hosts for potato pests.
management.environmental_control: Maintain balanced moisture during the critical tuber bulking stage.
management.professional_advice: Consult commercial potato extension specialists for petiole nitrate monitoring and vine kill timing.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Plant certified seed tubers and practice 3- to 4-year crop rotations with non-solanaceous crops.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Schedule irrigation to maintain 65%–75% available soil water capacity.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout fields twice weekly from emergence through vine kill for Colorado potato beetles and blight signs.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select locally adapted, high-yielding potato varieties with proven disease resistance packages.

overview.description: The specimen displays typical healthy raspberry foliage with pinnately compound leaves, serrated margins, white-tomentose undersides, and absence of cane blight, spur blight, or rust.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Compound leaves with 3 to 5 serrated leaflets, vibrant green upper surfaces, and characteristic silvery-white fuzzy undersides.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No purple spur blight lesions, yellow rust pustules, or anthracnose spotting present.
symptoms.progression: Sustains healthy primocane vegetative elongation and floricane berry production.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sunlight, well-drained fertile loam soil, cool temperate climate, and good organic mulch.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Heavy clay soil promotes Phytophthora root rot; wild brambles harbor viruses and orange rust.

management.cultural_practices: Trellis canes to maintain narrow hedgerows (12–18 inches wide); prune out spent floricanes immediately after summer fruiting.
management.sanitation: Destroy pruned canes to eliminate potential fungal inoculum; eliminate wild blackberries and raspberries within 600 feet.
management.environmental_control: Ensure raised planting beds to provide rapid drainage.
management.professional_advice: Consult small fruit extension specialists for virus screening and cane density management.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Maintain clean, weed-free hedgerows with wood chip or straw mulch.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation lines placed along the row base; keep all water off canes and leaves.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout primocanes in early summer for cane lesions and inspect foliage for spider mites.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant certified virus-free rootstock and cultivars resistant to root rot ('Boyne', 'Nova', 'Prelude').

overview.description: The specimen exhibits typical healthy soybean foliage with trifoliolate green leaves, smooth intact margins, and absence of frogeye leaf spot, soybean rust, or sudden death syndrome.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Trifoliolate leaves with three ovate to elliptic leaflets, uniform green coloration, and fine pubesence.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No angular frogeye spots, rust pustules, brown spot chlorosis, or interveinal necrosis present.
symptoms.progression: Sustains healthy vegetative growth through flowering (R1–R2) and pod filling (R5–R6).
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm growing season (70°F–85°F), full sun, well-aerated soil with active Bradyrhizobium nodulation, and adequate rainfall.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Potassium deficiency causes marginal yellowing; iron deficiency chlorosis occurs on high pH soils (>7.8).

management.cultural_practices: Inoculate seed with Bradyrhizobium japonicum in fields without recent soybean history; plant in 15- to 30-inch rows.
management.sanitation: Practice crop rotation with corn, wheat, or non-legume crops to disrupt soil-borne pathogens.
management.environmental_control: Optimize field drainage to prevent Phytophthora damping-off.
management.professional_advice: Consult agronomy extension specialists for economic thresholds on defoliating insects and pod diseases.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Clean combine harvesters when moving between fields to avoid spreading weed seeds or nematode cysts.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Manage irrigation to avoid waterlogging; match crop water demand during pod fill.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout fields weekly from vegetative stages through R6 for foliar diseases and soybean aphids.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select soybean varieties with resistance to soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Phytophthora root rot, and frogeye leaf spot.

overview.common_name: Powdery Mildew of Squash and Cucurbits
overview.description: Powdery mildew is the most common and destructive foliar disease of squash, pumpkins, and other cucurbits worldwide, covering leaves and petioles in a conspicuous white talcum-like fungal growth that causes rapid chlorosis, leaf death, and reduced fruit quality.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Circular, white powdery spots that develop initially on the lower (shaded) leaf surfaces and leaf petioles.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: White talcum-powder-like patches of superficial mycelia and conidia that rapidly coalesce to cover both upper and lower leaf surfaces; affected leaves turn yellow, then brown, brittle, and die prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Starts on older lower leaves after flowering and expands rapidly through the canopy; loss of foliage leads to sunscald on developing squash and poor sugar accumulation.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Leaf petioles, stems, and fruit handles (which become brown, shriveled, and brittle).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Podosphaera fusca) and Erysiphe cichoracearum
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (68°F–80°F / 20°C–27°C), dense shade, and high relative humidity (50%–90%); unlike most fungi, powdery mildew is actually inhibited by free water (rain) washing spores off leaves.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Airborne conidia carried long distances on wind currents; can germinate in humid air without free water droplets.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Dense canopy planting, heavy nitrogen fertilization, late-season plantings, and planting non-resistant cucurbit varieties.

management.cultural_practices: Space plants generously to maximize sunlight penetration and reduce canopy humidity. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization.
management.sanitation: Plow under or remove and compost infected crop residues immediately after harvest.
management.environmental_control: Plant in full sun; orient rows to take advantage of prevailing winds for canopy drying.
management.professional_advice: Consult vegetable extension specialists for bi-weekly fungicide spray schedules and to check for local strobilurin or DMI resistance.
management.general_treatments: Preventative biofungicides (potassium bicarbonate, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens), horticultural oils, or rotational targeted fungicides (quinoxyfen, cyflufenamid, metrafenone) initiated when first spots appear on lower leaves.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Eliminate volunteer squash and cucurbit weeds around field borders.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation lines exclusively; maintain plastic mulch to prevent plant contact with wet soil.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Inspect the undersides of the oldest crown leaves weekly beginning around bush flowering.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant powdery mildew-resistant (PMR) squash and pumpkin hybrids carrying genetic resistance (e.g., 'Success PMG', 'Romulus', 'Dunja').

overview.description: Leaf scorch is a widespread fungal foliar disease of strawberry that produces numerous small, irregular dark purple to brown spots across leaf blades, coalescing until entire leaves curl up and appear burned or scorched.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Numerous small (1–5 mm), irregular, purplish to dark red spots developing on the upper surfaces of leaves.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Unlike common leaf spot, leaf scorch spots remain dark purple without developing white or tan centers; as lesions multiply and coalesce, the entire leaf blade turns reddish-purple, curls at the margins, and dries to a burned, scorched brown.
symptoms.progression: Begins on older leaves in spring; during wet periods it rapidly spreads to all foliage, causing severe canopy scorch, weakened crown vigor, and small unmarketable fruit.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Leaf petioles, fruit pedicels, runners, and floral calyxes (sepals turn brown and brittle, ruining fruit presentation).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Diplocarpon earlianum (Ellis & Everh.) F.A. Wolf (anamorph Marssonina fragariae)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Moderate to warm temperatures (60°F–80°F / 15°C–27°C) accompanied by extended periods of leaf wetness (8–12+ hours) from rain or overhead sprinklers.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Rain splash and overhead irrigation water dispersing conidia from overwintered living infected leaves; airborne ascospores released from dead leaves in spring.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Overhead irrigation, dense matted row systems with poor airflow, excessive nitrogen fertilization, and planting susceptible varieties.

management.cultural_practices: Renovate matted-row plantings immediately after harvest by mowing foliage, narrowing rows, and rototilling between rows to incorporate leaf debris.
management.sanitation: Remove and destroy old infected leaves during spring bed cleanup before new growth emerges.
management.environmental_control: Maintain adequate spacing between strawberry plants on plasticulture raised beds to maximize airflow.
management.professional_advice: Consult strawberry extension specialists if severe calyx infection threatens fresh market berry saleability.
management.general_treatments: Protective fungicides (captan, thiram, or thiophanate-methyl) applied from early spring green-up through bloom.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Plant only certified disease-free strawberry crowns from reputable nurseries.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation lines underneath plastic mulch; avoid overhead sprinkler watering after establishment.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout older leaves in early spring and examine calyxes closely as fruit begins to size.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select resistant or tolerant strawberry cultivars (e.g., 'Allstar', 'Honeoye', 'Earliglow', 'Jewel'). Avoid highly susceptible cultivars ('Raritan', 'Redchief').

references.title: Foliar and Fruit Diseases of Strawberry

overview.description: The specimen exhibits typical healthy strawberry foliage with dark green trifoliolate leaves, sharply serrated margins, and absence of leaf spot, scorch, anthracnose, or powdery mildew.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Lush green trifoliolate leaves with distinct serrations, strong petioles, and uniform texture.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No purple spots, scorched leaf margins, gray mold, or powdery white fungal growth present.
symptoms.progression: Maintains vigorous crown growth, robust runner production, and continuous strawberry fruit sizing.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sunlight (8+ hours daily), raised beds with well-drained sandy loam soil, acidic pH (5.5–6.5), and consistent root moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Waterlogging promotes Phytophthora crown rot; excessive nitrogen produces dense foliage prone to Botrytis fruit rot.

management.cultural_practices: Plant on raised beds covered with black or silver plastic mulch; thin runners in day-neutral varieties to maintain crown vigor.
management.sanitation: Perform post-harvest renovation on Junebearing varieties by mowing leaves 2 inches above crowns and removing old plant debris.
management.environmental_control: Ensure well-drained soil to avoid root and crown diseases.
management.professional_advice: Consult small fruit extension specialists for petiole fertility monitoring and winter mulch timing.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Purchase certified disease-free, virus-indexed nursery plugs or dormant bare-root crowns.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Apply all irrigation via drip tape under plastic mulch to keep leaves and fruit completely dry.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout weekly for two-spotted spider mites, tarnished plant bugs, and foliar spots.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select disease-resistant strawberry cultivars adapted to your regional growing season.

overview.description: Bacterial spot is a widespread, destructive bacterial disease of tomato and pepper, causing small circular to angular water-soaked leaf spots, severe defoliation, blossom abortion, and raised scab-like fruit lesions.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small (1–3 mm), dark brown to black circular spots that appear water-soaked on lower surfaces and are frequently surrounded by a prominent yellow chlorotic halo.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions are dark brown, angular to circular, often coalescing during rainy weather; affected leaves turn yellow, scorch, and drop prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Spreads rapidly through tomato canopies during warm summer storms; extensive defoliation exposes green fruit to solar scald.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (small, raised, dark, scab-like or blister-like lesions that become sunken and cratered), sepals, and green stems.

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Xanthomonas perforans, X. vesicatoria, X. euvesicatoria, and X. gardneri
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75°F–86°F / 24°C–30°C), persistent high humidity, and driving rain or overhead sprinkler irrigation.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Infected seed, contaminated transplants, wind-driven rain splash, and handling wet plants.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Overhead irrigation, working in wet fields, and planting non-resistant commercial tomato cultivars.

management.cultural_practices: Rotate out of solanaceous crops for at least 2–3 years. Never handle or prune tomato plants when leaves are wet from dew or rain.
management.sanitation: Use hot-water treated or certified disease-free seed; destroy crop debris immediately following final harvest.
management.environmental_control: Stake and prune tomato plants to improve air circulation; use plastic mulch to prevent soil splash.
management.professional_advice: Consult vegetable extension specialists regarding copper-tolerant bacterial strains in your region.
management.general_treatments: Preventative fixed copper bactericides tank-mixed with mancozeb, or plant-activator sprays (acibenzolar-S-methyl) initiated early in the season.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Sterilize seedling trays, greenhouse benches, and trellising stakes before each season.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation lines exclusively; never use overhead sprinkler systems on tomatoes.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Inspect transplants thoroughly before field setting and scout rows weekly after rainfall.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select tomato varieties with identified resistance to Xanthomonas perforans races where available.

overview.description: Early blight is one of the most common and damaging foliar fungal diseases of tomato, producing characteristic dark brown circular spots with concentric target-board rings, severe lower-leaf defoliation, and stem cankers.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Dark brown to black spots developing initially on the oldest lower leaves, surrounded by a broad yellow chlorotic halo.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Circular to irregular necrotic lesions up to 1/2 inch in diameter featuring distinct, concentric ridges resembling a target board or tree growth rings.
symptoms.progression: Progresses steadily from the bottom of the plant upward; heavy blighting causes lower leaves to wither, dry up, and drop, exposing developing fruit to sunscald.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Stems (collar rot on seedlings, dark oval cankers on mature stems) and fruit (dark, leathery, sunken lesions near the stem attachment).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Alternaria linariae (formerly A. solani f. sp. lycopersici)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75°F–85°F / 24°C–29°C) with alternating periods of rain or heavy dew and dry sunny weather; plants stressed by heavy fruit loads are especially susceptible.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia; overwinters in infested tomato debris, solanaceous weeds (horsenettle, black nightshade), and volunteer tomatoes.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Lack of crop rotation, bottom leaves touching bare soil, overhead watering, and planting susceptible heirloom varieties.

management.cultural_practices: Rotate tomatoes out of the area for 2–3 years. Stake plants and prune lower leaves up to 12–18 inches above the soil once plants are established.
management.sanitation: Mulch soil with straw, compost, or plastic to prevent rain splash from soil to lower leaves; remove and destroy diseased crop debris at season's end.
management.environmental_control: Space plants generously (24–36 inches apart) to accelerate leaf drying.
management.professional_advice: Consult extension specialists to calibrate TomCast disease-forecasting spray schedules.
management.general_treatments: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper, or mancozeb) starting at first fruit set; rotate with biofungicides (Bacillus subtilis) under organic management.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Eradicate solanaceous weeds in and around the garden or field perimeter.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Water at the soil level using drip irrigation or soaker hoses; avoid wetting tomato foliage.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Inspect lower leaves weekly starting early in the summer.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant hybrid varieties carrying early blight resistance genes (e.g., 'Mountain Fresh Plus', 'Mountain Merit', 'Defiant PhR', 'Iron Lady', 'Plum Regal').

references.title: Early Blight in Tomato and Potato

overview.description: Late blight is a catastrophic oomycete disease of tomato and potato that can decimate entire plantings within days. It causes large, water-soaked, greasy lesions on leaves and stems, accompanied by white fuzzy mold on leaf undersides and destructive greasy fruit rot.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Large, irregular, pale green to water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand and turn dark brown to purplish-black.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions have an irregular, water-soaked, greasy appearance; in moist or humid weather, a distinctive delicate white downy or fuzzy growth develops on the undersides of leaves at the margins of lesions.
symptoms.progression: Under cool, wet conditions, the disease spreads with extreme speed, turning entire vines into a shriveled, blackened, rotting mass with a distinct pungent odor within 1 to 2 weeks.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Stems (dark brown greasy cankers causing sudden vine collapse) and fruit (large, firm, golden-brown to dark brown leathery patches that quickly rot).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (55°F–75°F / 13°C–24°C), relative humidity above 90%, and persistent leaf wetness from rain, dense fog, or heavy morning dew.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Airborne sporangia capable of traveling tens of miles on cloud-covered wind currents; rain splash; infected potato tubers or greenhouse transplants.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Cool, rainy, overcast weather; planting non-certified seed potatoes or greenhouse transplants carrying latent infection.

management.cultural_practices: Destroy confirmed late blight-infected plants immediately: pull plants, bag them in plastic on a sunny day to solarize, and dispose of them in municipal trash (do not compost).
management.sanitation: Eliminate volunteer potatoes and tomatoes; eradicate nightshade weeds.
management.environmental_control: Locate plantings in full sun away from low frost pockets or persistent fog areas.
management.professional_advice: Late blight is a reportable, community-threatening pathogen; alert your county extension office immediately upon discovery to protect regional growers.
management.general_treatments: Protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper) must be applied preventatively before spores arrive; once systemic infection occurs, organic treatments are ineffective.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Inspect all purchased tomato transplants meticulously for brown stem lesions before planting.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Never use overhead watering; keep foliage completely dry using ground drip lines.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Check national disease tracking alerts at USAblight.org; scout plants twice weekly during cool, rainy weather.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant late-blight resistant cultivars possessing Ph-2 and Ph-3 genes (e.g., 'Defiant PhR', 'Mountain Merit', 'Iron Lady', 'Mountain Magic', 'Plum Regal').

references.title: Late Blight of Tomato and Potato

overview.description: Tomato leaf mold is a foliar fungal disease that thrives in high-humidity environments, especially in greenhouses, high tunnels, and sheltered gardens, producing pale chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces and velvety olive-brown mold on leaf undersides.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Pale green to yellow-green diffuse spots with indistinct margins appearing on the upper surfaces of older leaves.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Directly beneath the yellow spots on the underside of the leaf, a dense, velvety, olive-green to grayish-brown mat of fungal spores develops. Infected leaves yellow, curl, wither, and drop prematurely.
symptoms.progression: Originates on the oldest leaves in the lower canopy and spreads rapidly upward under sustained high relative humidity.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Blossoms (which abort, reducing fruit set); rarely green fruit (causing black stem-end rot).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Passalora fulva (Cooke) U. Braun & Crous (syn. Cladosporium fulvum)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70°F–75°F / 21°C–24°C) coupled with high relative humidity (>85%); uncommon in open fields with low humidity and good airflow.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Airborne conidia transported by air currents, splashing water, insects, and contaminated tools or clothing; overwinters in crop debris or greenhouse structures as conidia or sclerotial bodies.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: High tunnel and greenhouse production without adequate ventilation, dense planting, and planting susceptible varieties lacking Cf resistance genes.

management.cultural_practices: Maximize ventilation in greenhouses and high tunnels using exhaust fans, ridge vents, and horizontal airflow fans. Maintain humidity below 85%.
management.sanitation: Clean and disinfect greenhouse frames and ground sheets between crops; remove and destroy lower diseased foliage.
management.environmental_control: Space tomato plants widely (minimum 18–24 inches in rows) and prune lower suckers to maintain canopy airflow.
management.professional_advice: Consult commercial greenhouse vegetable specialists for Cf-gene race compatibility.
management.general_treatments: Preventative biofungicides (Bacillus subtilis, copper hydroxide, potassium bicarbonate) or targeted fungicides (chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin) applied when humidity is high.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Remove all solanaceous debris from high tunnels at the end of each production cycle.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation lines exclusively; heat and vent greenhouses before sundown to prevent overnight condensation on leaves.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Inspect the undersides of lower leaves weekly in high tunnels and greenhouses.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select tomato cultivars carrying Cladosporium fulvum resistance genes (e.g., Cf-4, Cf-9, e.g., 'Rebelina', 'Maxifort', 'Geronimo').

references.title: Tomato Leaf Mold in High Tunnels and Greenhouses

overview.description: Septoria leaf spot is one of the most destructive foliar fungal diseases of tomato in warm, wet summer climates, producing numerous small, circular spots with dark margins and ash-gray centers containing tiny black pycnidia, causing severe lower canopy defoliation.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Dozens of small (1.5 to 3 mm), circular spots that develop on the oldest lower leaves following rainfall.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Spots have dark brown to black circular borders with pale ash-gray or tan centers; using a hand lens, tiny black specks (fungal fruiting bodies called pycnidia) are visible embedded in the gray centers.
symptoms.progression: Heavily infected leaves turn yellow, curl up, wither, and drop off; defoliation moves rapidly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving plants with bare lower stems and sunscalded fruit.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Leaf petioles, stems, and flower calyxes; fruit is rarely infected directly, but fruit yield and quality plummet.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Moderate to warm temperatures (68°F–77°F / 20°C–25°C) combined with high humidity and extended periods of rainfall or overhead watering.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Rain splash and overhead irrigation droplets splashing fungal spores from infested crop debris onto lower foliage; tools, equipment, and hands moving through wet plants.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Lack of crop rotation, lower leaves touching bare soil, overhead watering, and weed hosts (horsenettle, nightshade).

management.cultural_practices: Rotate tomatoes away from previous solanaceous locations for at least 2–3 years. Stake or cage plants and prune lower foliage up to 12 inches above the soil.
management.sanitation: Apply 2 to 3 inches of clean straw, paper, or plastic mulch around plant bases to prevent soil splash; remove and bag infected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear.
management.environmental_control: Space plants at least 24 to 36 inches apart in full sun to ensure rapid drying after rain.
management.professional_advice: Consult local cooperative extension vegetable specialists for disease-forecasting thresholds.
management.general_treatments: Protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper, or mancozeb) applied every 7 to 10 days starting at transplant establishment or first blossom set.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Meticulously clean up and dispose of all tomato vines at the end of the season; do not till diseased vines into the garden bed.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Deliver water exclusively through drip irrigation or soaker hoses; never use overhead sprinklers.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Examine lower leaves weekly starting in early summer, especially after rainy weather.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Most heirloom and standard varieties are susceptible; plant tolerant varieties (e.g., 'Iron Lady', 'Mountain Magic', 'Jasper') that show delayed disease progression.

overview.description: The two-spotted spider mite is a prolific microscopic arachnid pest that feeds on plant sap by piercing individual plant cells on leaf undersides, producing widespread chlorotic stippling, bronzing, fine silken webbing, and rapid leaf desiccation under hot, dry conditions.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Minute yellow or white stippling (pinpoint flecking) across the upper leaf surface caused by mites piercing cells on the underside.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: As feeding progresses, stippled areas coalesce, causing leaves to turn pale yellow, then bronze or dusty gray, become papery, and die. Fine silken webbing covers leaf undersides and terminal growing points.
symptoms.progression: Mite populations explode under hot, dry conditions (completing a generation in 5–7 days); severe webbing can engulf entire shoot terminals and reduce plant vigor dramatically.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Stems, flowers (which desiccate and drop), and fruit (stunted growth, yellow flecking, and sunscald from defoliation).

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Hot, dry, and dusty weather (temperatures above 85°F / 30°C and low relative humidity); drought-stressed plants are especially preferred.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind dispersal via silken threads ('ballooning'); crawling between touching leaves; hitchhiking on workers' clothing and tools.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Over-use of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroid or carbamate insecticides that kill beneficial predatory mites; drought stress and dusty field roads.

management.cultural_practices: Avoid plant drought stress by maintaining adequate, regular irrigation. Suppress dust along field borders by watering dirt roadways.
management.sanitation: Destroy heavily infested plants at field edges before mites disperse across the field; eradicate broadleaf weeds that host overwintering mites.
management.environmental_control: Introduce or conserve natural predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus) and predatory insects (lady beetles, minute pirate bugs).
management.professional_advice: Consult extension entomologists for miticide resistance management; two-spotted spider mites rapidly develop resistance to chemical classes.
management.general_treatments: Insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils (1–2% neem or paraffinic oil), sulfur (do not apply within 30 days of oil or above 90°F), or selective miticides (bifenazate, abamectin).

prevention.crop_hygiene: Clear weed hosts (especially morning glory and pigweed) adjacent to tomato plantings before the growing season.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Maintain consistent drip irrigation to eliminate drought stress; periodic overhead misting in home gardens can physically disrupt mite webbing.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Check leaf undersides weekly with a 10x hand lens, tapping leaves over a white sheet of paper to detect moving specks.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Some wild tomato accessions (Solanum habrochaites) possess glandular trichomes that deter spider mites; commercial varieties vary in tolerance.

references.title: Spider Mites Pest Management Guidelines - Tomato
Two-Spotted Spider Mite Management on Tomato

overview.description: Target spot is a destructive fungal disease affecting tomatoes in warm, humid tropical and subtropical production regions, causing circular pinpoint spots that expand into zonate brown lesions, severe defoliation, and deep pitted lesions on green and ripe fruit.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Small, pinpoint brown spots on upper leaf surfaces that expand into circular lesions with light brown centers and dark brown concentric rings.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Lesions are circular to irregular (3–10 mm) with distinct dark margins and lighter tan centers, often resembling early blight but lacking the broad chlorotic halos; spots often crack or drop out.
symptoms.progression: Initiates in the lower canopy and progresses rapidly upward during periods of high humidity and rainfall, leading to extensive canopy blighting and defoliation.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (small, dark, sunken circular lesions that become crater-like with gray-white fungal centers) and stems.

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Corynespora cassiicola (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) C.T. Wei
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (68°F–86°F / 20°C–30°C) with persistent high humidity (80%–100%) and prolonged leaf wetness (16–24 hours).
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia; survives in crop residue, volunteer tomatoes, and numerous alternative weed hosts (e.g., sicklepod, croton).
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Dense canopy growth, poor ventilation, overhead irrigation, and continuous production in warm subtropical regions.

management.cultural_practices: Maintain wide plant spacing and prune lower foliage up to the first flower cluster to encourage air movement. Avoid planting consecutive tomato crops.
management.sanitation: Destroy crop residues immediately after harvest; eliminate broadleaf weed hosts around field margins.
management.environmental_control: Utilize plastic mulch to prevent splash transmission from soil and maintain row orientation parallel to prevailing winds.
management.professional_advice: Consult local university extension vegetable pathologists for regional fungicide efficacy updates and resistance warnings.
management.general_treatments: Protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) applied before disease establishment; rotational sprays of boscalid, fluxapyroxad, or azoxystrobin.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Ensure complete destruction and incorporation of old crop residues between growing seasons.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Deliver irrigation strictly through drip lines beneath plastic mulch.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout lower canopy leaves weekly, particularly during warm, rainy summer stretches.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Commercial tomato cultivars show varying tolerance; consult seed distributors for varieties with improved target spot field tolerance.

overview.description: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus is one of the most economically devastating viral diseases of tomato worldwide, transmitted persistently by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly, causing extreme stunting, upward leaf curling, marginal chlorosis, and total cessation of marketable fruit production.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Severe upward cupping and curling of leaflet margins, reduction in leaf size, and conspicuous yellowing (chlorosis) along leaflet margins and interveinal areas.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Leaves are small, puckered, crumpled, and cupped upward into a spoon-like shape; terminal growth becomes dense, bushy, and stunted.
symptoms.progression: Infected young plants become severely stunted; flowers drop prematurely, resulting in nearly 100% loss of fruit production if infected early in the season.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Floral buds (flower abortion) and stems (shortened internodes causing a compact, bushy 'bonsai' appearance); fruit already set remains small and unmarketable.

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV, family Geminiviridae, genus Begomovirus)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry climates (temperatures above 75°F / 24°C) that favor rapid population growth and dispersal of whitefly insect vectors.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Transmitted in a persistent, circulative manner by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci (sweetpotato whitefly, MEAM1 and MED cryptic species); not transmitted mechanically or through seeds.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: High whitefly populations, proximity to infected winter tomato or weed hosts, and planting susceptible non-resistant cultivars.

management.cultural_practices: Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately upon early symptom recognition to prevent them from serving as virus reservoirs. Install 50-mesh insect screening in greenhouses.
management.sanitation: Maintain a 2- to 3-month regional tomato-free period to break the whitefly-virus cycle; eliminate weed hosts (nightshade, mallow) around field perimeters.
management.environmental_control: Use reflective silver or metallic plastic mulches to deter whiteflies from landing on young tomato seedlings.
management.professional_advice: Consult agricultural extension entomologists for whitefly biotype identification and coordinated area-wide vector management.
management.general_treatments: Vector management using systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) at transplanting, followed by rotational foliar sprays (spiromesifen, cyantraniliprole, pyriproxyfen) or insecticidal soaps.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Plant exclusively certified virus-free transplants produced under insect-proof screenhouses.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Standard drip irrigation; avoid drought stress that exacerbates viral stunting.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Monitor whitefly adult populations weekly using yellow sticky traps and inspecting leaflet undersides.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Planting resistant or tolerant tomato hybrids carrying Ty-1, Ty-3, or Ty-5 resistance genes (e.g., 'Tycoon', 'Charger', 'Grand Slam', 'Tribute', 'Gurney's Invincible') is the primary and most reliable defense.

references.title: Management of Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus in Tomato
Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus Guidelines

overview.description: Tomato mosaic virus is an extremely stable, highly infectious tobamovirus that spreads mechanically through touching, pruning tools, and tobacco products, causing mottled green mosaic patterns, distorted strapping ('shoestring') leaves, and internal brown fruit necrosis.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Mottling of leaves with alternating light green and dark green mosaic patches, accompanied by leaf distortion, curling, and crinkling.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: Light and dark green mosaic pattern; in severe cases, leaf blades become severely reduced, distorted, or strapped into a thin 'fern-leaf' or 'shoestring' appearance.
symptoms.progression: Varies with temperature and virus strain; cool conditions accentuate mosaic mottling, while hot conditions produce stunting, leaf curling, and severe yield reduction.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: Fruit (patchy ripening, yellow rings, and internal browning of the fruit wall known as vascular browning or brownwall).

causes_and_spread.causal_organism: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV, family Virgaviridae, genus Tobamovirus)
causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Any temperature supporting tomato growth; the virus is exceptionally stable and withstands temperatures up to 194°F (90°C) and can persist for years in dry plant debris.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Mechanical transmission through handling, grafting, pruning tools, trellising, worker clothing, and tobacco products; seed-borne on the seed coat.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Smoking or using tobacco products before handling plants (tobacco can harbor tobamoviruses), unsterilized pruning shears, and planting susceptible heirloom cultivars.

management.cultural_practices: Workers must wash hands with soap and water or nonfat dry milk (20%) before and during plant handling. Prohibit smoking or tobacco use in greenhouses and fields.
management.sanitation: Dip pruning shears and tools in a 10% household bleach or 20% nonfat milk solution between plants; rogue out and bag infected plants immediately upon detection.
management.environmental_control: Isolate suspect plants to prevent physical contact with adjacent healthy vines.
management.professional_advice: Consult diagnostic plant pathology laboratories for serological (ELISA) or molecular (PCR) confirmation to differentiate ToMV from TMV and ToBRFV.
management.general_treatments: There are no curative chemical or biological treatments for viral infections once established inside plant tissue.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Plant exclusively certified disease-free, hot-water treated or trisodium phosphate (TSP)-treated seeds.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Use drip irrigation; ensure hoses and equipment do not physically abrade leaves.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout transplants and young plants weekly for mosaic mottling and leaf strapping.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Plant hybrid varieties carrying the Tm-1, Tm-2, or Tm-2^2 resistance alleles (labeled 'T' or 'ToMV' resistant on seed packets).

references.title: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) and Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV)
Tomato Mosaic Virus and Tobacco Mosaic Virus

overview.description: The specimen displays typical healthy tomato foliage with lush green compound leaves, defined serration, aromatic glandular hairs, and absence of bacterial spot, early/late blight, leaf mold, or viral mosaic.

symptoms.leaf_symptoms: Vibrant, uniform dark green compound leaves with crisp serrated margins and sturdy erect petioles.
symptoms.lesion_appearance: No target-board spots, water-soaked lesions, white sporulation, yellow mottling, or leaf curling observed.
symptoms.progression: Sustains healthy indeterminate or determinate vine growth, robust flower truss formation, and uniform fruit set.
symptoms.other_parts_affected: None.

causes_and_spread.favorable_conditions: Full sun (6–8+ hours), daytime temperatures of 70°F–85°F (21°C–29°C), well-drained loam soil rich in organic matter (pH 6.2–6.8), and consistent moisture.
causes_and_spread.transmission_modes: Not applicable.
causes_and_spread.susceptibility_factors: Over-fertilization with nitrogen can delay flowering; irregular watering causes blossom-end rot and fruit cracking.

management.cultural_practices: Stake, cage, or trellis plants to elevate foliage off the ground; prune suckers to balance vegetative and reproductive growth.
management.sanitation: Apply 2–3 inches of straw, wood chips, or plastic mulch around the plant base; prune lower leaves touching the soil.
management.environmental_control: Ensure adequate spacing (24–36 inches) between plants to maximize air movement.
management.professional_advice: Consult local cooperative extension specialists for soil test interpretation and blossom-end rot calcium management.
management.general_treatments: No pesticide applications needed for healthy foliage.

prevention.crop_hygiene: Sterilize stakes and cages with a 10% bleach solution between seasons.
prevention.irrigation_practices: Water exclusively at the base using drip irrigation or soaker hoses; never wet tomato foliage.
prevention.monitoring_and_scouting: Scout plants twice weekly from transplanting through harvest for hornworms, aphids, and early leaf spots.
prevention.resistant_varieties: Select disease-resistant hybrid cultivars labeled VFN (Verticillium, Fusarium, Nematodes) or with late blight and viral resistance.
